summary:
Abuja Federal Capital Territory stands under Nigeria's national framework with no territorial carve-out. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reinforces colonial-era offences of "carnal knowledge against the order of nature" punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment, and its own provisions carry 10 to 14 years for same-sex cohabitation, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advisory, as reported by Sahara Reporters, adds that the law reaches people who help arrange or conduct same-sex marriages and criminalises activities involving gay groups and organisations.

The same advisory warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, and states that some states operating under Sharia law can impose the death penalty. Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that police have used the 2014 Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrest, and that the statute reaches far beyond marriage.

A trans visitor should treat the territory as a place where a documented killing has gone unpunished. On 8 August 2024 the beaten, bruised body of 33-year-old transgender TikToker "Abuja Area Mama" was found along the Katampe-Mabushi expressway in the Banex/Wuse II area of Abuja, hours after she posted a final video and having previously expressed fear for her life. A police statement described the victim as "a man fully dressed in female clothing with no means of identification". The Abuja police chief, Benneth Igweh, ordered a thorough and discreet investigation; six months later no suspects had been charged. A petition of nearly 6,000 signatures demands investigation of the killing as a hate crime, and a human-rights group has sued the national government and the police for failing to investigate, seeking a court order compelling investigation and prosecution after multiple petitions were ignored.

Everyday enforcement is extortionate and violent. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing, which makes dating apps an active entrapment vector rather than a social convenience.

Gender presentation carries exposure independent of identity documents. There is no legal route in Nigeria to change gender. Cross-dressing is banned under Sharia law in twelve states and in the Nigerian military, and Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live under fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available. Police in the Area Mama case recorded her as a man in female clothing, indicating how an officer's report can fix a trans person's legal status at the scene.

Detention carries a further uncertainty: placement between male and female sections is left to official discretion. Press coverage at the sentencing of Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye) openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in.
tangentialFactors:
The territory's record is not a standalone incident but an instance of the national floor: Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the 2014 Act reinforced colonial-era criminalisation rather than replacing it. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's advisory warns of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law, which places Nigerian travel guidance among the most severe issued by foreign governments.

Mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common across Nigeria, especially in the twelve states operating under Sharia law, according to BBC News (9 August 2024). The Area Mama killing is distinguished less by its brutality than by the official response: a promised thorough and discreet investigation, no charges after six months, ignored petitions, and litigation brought specifically to compel the state to act.

Institutions outside the police also restrict gender presentation. Cross-dressing bans apply under Sharia law in twelve states and within the Nigerian military, and proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public have circulated at national level since at least September 2022. A foreign government advisory covering movement restrictions adds a further layer: breaching curfews or movement controls can itself lead to arrest and detention.
localsOnly:
Residents live with a statute that criminalises the ordinary conduct of a household. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 bans same-sex marriage and civil unions, same-sex cohabitation, public display of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and Human Rights Watch documents its use to justify torture and arbitrary arrest by police.

There is no legal mechanism to change gender on Nigerian documents. Under Sharia law in twelve states, same-sex acts between men and between women are criminalised and male sodomy carries the death penalty under state Zina provisions; cross-dressing is banned there and in the Nigerian military.

Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations against her but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Community response to the Area Mama killing has been organised rather than silent: a petition of nearly 6,000 signatures demands investigation as a hate crime, and a human-rights group has sued the national government and the police for failing to investigate. Reporting on Abuja's queer scene documents threats and raids alongside informal community organising.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing reported in September 2022 have been enacted is unresolved in the sources available; the inventory does not settle their legislative status.

Whether the killing of Abuja Area Mama is legally established as a hate crime is unresolved. The petition asserts that characterisation, and no charges had been brought six months after the killing.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 advisory is a national-level warning with no Abuja-specific breakdown, and the sources do not state whether the Federal Capital Territory itself falls under any Sharia-based capital-penalty provision or only under the secular layer.

Whether the police investigation ordered by Benneth Igweh continued beyond the six-month point reported by The Dial is not sourced here, and no outcome of the human-rights group's lawsuit against the national government and the police is recorded in the inventory.

Whether a trans visitor's entry documents are examined for gender markers at Nigerian border posts is not addressed by any source in this inventory.
